analysis.one_liner: Lets multinational companies bring offshore profits home at a sharply reduced tax rate.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, vote, or committee action after its referral to the House Ways and Means Committee and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let U.S. corporations deduct most or all of the dividends they receive from their foreign subsidiaries, cutting the federal tax rate on money brought back from abroad from the standard 35% corporate rate to roughly 5.25%, or zero if the company promises to spend the money domestically on research, facilities, or manufacturing. The company's own executives, not any government agency, would approve the reinvestment plan. It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Large multinational corporations holding untaxed profits in foreign subsidiaries would gain the most: they could move those profits into the U.S. while paying an effective federal tax rate of about 5.25%, instead of 35%, and pay effectively nothing on dividends they pledge to reinvest domestically under a plan approved by their own officers. Companies whose foreign earnings were already destined for domestic research, plant, or startup spending would get a windfall for behavior they would likely have pursued anyway.

how_it_helps.text: Companies electing the bill could deduct 85% of dividends received from foreign subsidiaries, reducing the effective federal tax rate on repatriated earnings from the 35% corporate rate to roughly 5.25%.

Companies that reinvest the dividends within three years under a 'qualified domestic reinvestment plan' — covering research and development, facility expansion, proof-of-concept centers, early-stage venture capital, or manufacturing startup costs — could deduct 100%, paying no federal tax on those repatriated earnings.
The bill eliminates the existing dollar limitation on the deduction, so there would be no cap on how much repatriated profit a company could bring home at the reduced rate.

The reinvestment plan would only need approval from the taxpayer's own president or chief executive and its board of directors; no federal agency would review or certify how the money was actually spent.

analysis.who_pays: The U.S. Treasury would bear the cost in reduced tax collections, since corporate income that would otherwise be taxed at the full 35% rate would arrive at roughly 5% or nothing. Revenue lost on a one-time tax holiday must be made up by other taxpayers, by borrowing, or by forgoing federal spending; the 2004 version of this same tax holiday, which the bill re-creates, was followed by studies finding most of the repatriated cash went to share buybacks and dividends rather than new hiring.

drawbacks.text: The deduction directly reduces federal corporate tax revenue on earnings that would otherwise be taxed at the full rate, shifting the burden onto other taxpayers or adding to the deficit.

The 100%-deduction reinvestment option requires no federal oversight: a plan is 'qualified' if approved by the company's own CEO and board, creating no mechanism to verify that the money produced new domestic investment rather than substituting for spending already planned.

By making the holiday available to the taxpayer's prior and current tax years with no dollar cap, the bill would reward companies that had shifted the most profits offshore, rather than conditioning the benefit on any new hiring or investment commitment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a genuine but narrow benefit — faster repatriation of offshore cash — while its main effect is a large, one-time transfer of tax liability from multinationals to the Treasury. The reinvestment requirement looks like a condition but is enforced only through self-certification, and the comparable 2004 tax holiday is widely documented to have produced mostly buybacks and dividends rather than jobs, which is why later proposals of this type drew sustained scrutiny. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill trades a large revenue loss for an uncertain, likely modest, economic gain.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Brian Bilbray introduced the bill in the House on March 11, 2011, with a single Republican cosponsor.
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means the same day, which was the only congressional action the bill ever received.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the bill's complete action history before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers and the Treasury are better off because the bill died: the federal government continues to tax repatriated offshore earnings at the full corporate rate rather than collecting roughly 5 cents on the dollar. Multinationals with large offshore cash piles lost their chance at a one-time windfall, though the question returned repeatedly in later Congresses.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 11, 2011 and never scheduled a hearing or vote; the bill sat there until Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only Republicans appear in the record — the sponsor and one cosponsor — and no votes were ever taken, so no party breakdown exists.

industries.industry: Large multinational corporations with untaxed offshore profits
industries.note: The bill would let them repatriate foreign earnings at roughly 5.25% instead of 35%, or at 0% under a self-certified reinvestment plan, converting tax they would otherwise owe into retained cash. The cost lands on the Treasury and other taxpayers, with no federal verification that the money was newly invested.
They would not qualify for the deduction but would share the burden of the lost federal revenue through other taxes, borrowing, or reduced spending.
